item.title: Many Such Takes: Thanksgiving Canceled, Millennial Marriage, Pit Bulls (Again) and More
item.description: The most unhinged discourse of the week, always free
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Many Such Takes, my twice-monthly roundup of Internet drama and discourse (mostly Twitter) and funny happenings online. If you enjoy a good guilty pleasure of unhinged discourse, this is for you. If it’s not your kind of thing, I implore you to check out my other recent articles, because while publishing 4-5 times a week, there’s always something for someone:

  • Relationships: Why don’t women make the first move?

  • Social dynamics: Why I gave up on throwing big parties

  • Fashion: 21 Outfits I wore in Paris this July

  • Personal essay: My “secret club” at theater camp got me in a lot of trouble

  • Parenting: Is it “outsourcing” to occasionally get help with your kids?

  • More relationships: Is the stereotype of women being “clingy” about marriage and babies still true?

While MST will always be free, the rest of my content—4 articles per week—are paid. As I said before, it’s a little bit of everything—mostly social dynamics (dating, friendship, marriage, etc) but also some fashion, and some random shower thoughts questions like what happened to picky eaters in olden times? If that sounds appealing, consider becoming a paid subscriber. I’m running a 30% off sale on annual subscriptions for the next week! (Even at my regular prices, I have some of the lowest $-for-article volume pricing on Substack, but a summer sale can’t hurt.)

Get 30% off forever

Thanksgiving Canceled

Time for some good old fashioned Woke 1 discourse! Francesca Hong is a candidate running for governor of Wisconsin, and this week, some particularly memorable past moments of hers came to light. First, she previously described having a half-white son (who was presumably sired by the white guy she married) as an uncomfortable “proximity to whiteness.”

But most of the ire this week came from the fact that in 2020 (who amongst us was not a little insane in 2020) she proposed canceling Thanksgiving due to trauma imposed on indigenous “folx” by pilgrims who weren’t WEARING A FUCKING MASK:

I feel weird defending anything about this tweet, but considering it was 2020, “cancel Thanksgiving” likely didn’t mean getting rid of the holiday entirely, but staying home during that particular Thanksgiving. I’m sure many of you also think that’s stupid, but there is a meaningful difference between “canceling” in the covid sense, and cancellation.

But, as it turns out, she has ragged on basically every holiday, including a line about feeling “attacked” when non-consensually exposed to a Christmas-related imagery via a computer background:

So, how is she going to do damage control? During a relatively softball interview, she did a 180 and declared that while she is a bit of a “curmudgeon” about most holidays, her favorite holiday is Thanksgiving after all! Just say you hate indigenous folx and go. She then went on to very vaguely and oddly describe Thanksgiving in a way that only someone who never celebrated it would, summing it up as a “big event,” with very little detail indicating any real familiarity.

As I said, she talks about Thanksgiving the way Trump talks about the Bible.

More good takes:

Subscribe now

Millennial Marriage

I was happy to see this topic in the discourse because this had been my beat for ages now. Some of my fellow millennial women pointed out that conversations about women of their generation “delaying marriage” are incongruent with the experiences of secular millennial women in the 2000s and 2010s: being called crazy if you wanted any commitment at all, with the understanding that men didn’t want to be married and would put it off as long as possible. Now, suddenly, women have “delayed!”

While I’m sure some women deliberately deprioritized marriage to focus on other things, my anecdotal experience of being a millennial woman was that nearly every woman wanted marriage more than her boyfriend did (a lot of time, even admitting you wanted a monogamous boyfriend made you seem “crazy”) and that anti-marriage sentiment was popular among lots of young men, not just the ones with options.

I wrote about this exact phenomenon here

This (very apt) tweet seems to have started the discourse:

Followed by this one, which really kicked shit off:

I maintain Lisa is correct! At least where I grew up, it was considered “crazy” to even mention you wanted to get married at some point, even if you were well into your twenties! Dating for marriage was considered so unhinged and weird that you would have to pretend you weren’t doing it, even when dating relatively older guys. I had a male friend in his early thirties—not particularly Chadly or tall or good with women, just a regular guy—who stopped seeing a woman because she mentioned marriage too early on, even though it was more generally speaking and not about marrying him specifically. Another friend (age 38 at the time) advised my husband to never live with a woman or get married, right after we got engaged (nice.) Anyway, MANY SUCH CASES!

I will say the trend seems to be shifting a bit, and Gen Z men do seem a bit more interested in marriage than their female counterparts, although things probably haven’t changed as much as trad Twitter would have you think. More about that here:

Subscribe now

Primetime

In case you missed it, there’s a A24 new movie on the horizon—Primetime, based on the career of Chris Hansen of To Catch a Predator fame. Chris Hansen will be played by none other than Robert Pattinson who does a…fairly convincing Chris Hansen impression despite not looking very much like him.

But perhaps the best Primetime discourse came from this tweet, which takes issue with the fact that a talented actor fell so far that he was “forced” to play a pedophile:

I couldn’t help but feel I was getting shades of “Sydney Sweeney is a pedophile because she played a character who sucked on a binky during a sexy video in Euphoria.”

This sparked some pretty entertaining responses:

But perhaps the best tweet about this movie came from this person, with 81K likes and counting:

Subscribe now

Survyeys

I interrupt this programming to ask you to fill out my anonymous surveys!

Consider:

  • This one about socialization

  • This one about dating and politics

  • This one about first dates

Pit Bulls (Again)

I am obviously no stranger to “aggressive dog discourse.” I was never a big pit bull person, but also didn’t care that much either way. I thought about pit bulls about as much as I thought about the Steelers, which is to say, almost never. If the topic came up, I mostly bought into the “it’s the owner, not the dog” thing because it was the line that was parroted around me constantly, and I even had people telling me it was racist—not dog-racist, but like, actually racist, somehow, to believe dog breeds had any inherently different traits despite being bred specifically for different traits, unlike humans.

Until I had kids. Suddenly, there were a bunch of pit bulls (often unleashed!) roaming around my neighborhood, and I was increasingly aware of just how badly that can go when little kids are involved. My husband was chased and nearly bitten by one on his run, and when he yelled at the owner for losing control of her dog, she burst into tears and was comforted by bystanders who thought my husband was a big ol’ meanie. Frequently, I cross the street to get away from one, and its owner yells after me that “she’s friendly,” as if I’m supposed to know that (or believe them, which, I don’t.) I’ve seen stories of pit bulls with aggressive histories erased and pushed onto families, only to kill their children. I’m aware that shelters are passing off pit bulls as other breeds to sanitize them for families who otherwise may have safety concerns. Consider me radicalized.

Now, I’m at the point where I view pit bulls more or less as domesticated tigers or assault rifles with their own free will, carrying a small chance they will randomly just snap and kill someone for no reason. Because, well, they sometimes do that, even when they’re raised by attentive, loving suburban families who would never abuse an animal. So much for “the owner.” As for chihuahuas being more aggressive, they have yet to kill anyone!

All that to say, this is basically the only Twitter hivemind topics where I think Twitter is much more sane and reasonable than the general population, who mostly, across political lines, believe that pit bulls are totally fine to allow around children because they have one and hasn’t eaten anyone yet. Well, pediatricians apparently disagree. But that doesn’t matter. Outside of Twitter, people think it’s crazy to be concerned about having your children around these things.

In case that rant somehow wasn’t enough for you, you can read more of my thoughts on the topic here.

But anyway, pit bulls are back in the Twitter discourse, because why not! They seem to connect everyone across the political spectrum, not easy to do on a place like X The Everything App, where nearly any position on any topic can have you hounded by people who are one crashout away from being sectioned.

I’ve rounded up some of the most insane/amusing takes, such as this guy who suggests that a child fleeing a pit bull should simply learn to stop being so afraid and the dog is only aggressively chasing them because they can smell fear (if this were true—and it may very well be—it’s an unintentionally great argument for “pit bulls are unsafe around children.”)

I can’t stop thinking about Crazy Zeke:

This one might take the cake for “bad takes:” If you live near a wacko who lets their pit bull roam free, the onus should be on you and your children to shelter in place indefinitely:

This is why I come to Twitter:

Anyway, because this invariably always comes back to “Other things are more dangerous” (and, based on deaths alone, yes) I will just leave this here:

I loled:

Funny Tweets/Other Happenings

For a while this particular video of a contestant from the TLC show, Match Me Abroad, was going viral on Twitter. I guarantee you that it goes in a very different direction than you’re expecting:

A good old fashioned parenting tweet:

Monitoring this situation:

And, last but not least, a “we should go to war” post from a man who is living in a country that is involved in wars, has an army, and has suspiciously not joined said army. Apparently, billions must die because of…*checks notes* too many men being stay-at-home boyfriends.

item.title: In Defense of Silly Little Rules
item.description: How I was radicalized by the bedlam of Disneyland
item.content:encoded:
This article is free, but most of my 4-5 weekly articles are paid, so consider becoming a free or paid subscriber if you enjoy it!

This summer, my husband and I took our kids to Disneyland Paris. It was my first Disney trip since a Los Angeles family trip when I was twelve, when the caricature artist painted a comically enormous chin on me, only to revise it after my mom whispered, “That’s an insecurity of hers,” to him.

But anyway.

Disneyland Paris is not as intense as Disneyworld in Orlando (where I’ve actually never been, I’m a bit scared.) Disneyland Paris is much smaller, much cheaper, and it’s a day trip because you can get there on a forty-minute train, provided you are in Paris to begin with. (I am aware at this point, someone might say something like, “Wow, real OUT OF TOUCH, assuming EVERYONE is always in Paris.” Privilege checked!)

But one thing about Disneyland Paris which is the same as any Disney location? There is a lot of waiting. And not just waiting—waiting with children who don’t always understand why they have to wait. We took an early morning train so we would arrive before it opened, figuring this was our only chance to take our daughter on the very popular Frozen ride. The wait time for that ride was already over an hour before the park opened. So with this reality check in mind, we expected to wait a lot, and warned our kids that being bored in line was the price they’d pay for fun rides. Our kids whined a little, but complied.

But you know who didn’t comply? Certain poorly-behaved adults.

As we waited at the front gates for the park to open (at which point we could swipe our tickets and start waiting for rides) we noticed that everyone was basically cooperating, fully aware that waiting was part of the deal, except for four adults in their twenties wearing Mickey Mouse ears and backpacks, who frantically scampered past the line, giggling. They were convinced that they had figured out the “one secret trick” to avoiding the wait times at Disney—just break the rules, while hoping everyone else follows them.

Nobody did anything about it. They had cut a bunch of families, for the most part, and none of us were looking to brawl—or worse, be a Karen. They cut everyone, probably entered the ride lines before everyone else, and did the whole thing without a hint of shame.

Later, when we were waiting for a ride, we noticed there was a single rider line, where people riding alone could fill spare spots and enjoy shorter wait times. My husband noticed four young women pretending not to know each other in the line, then laughing and performing a taunting dance together when the ride attendants weren’t looking, basking in the victory of having fooled them. Immediately, the attendant noticed what they were doing and kicked them out of the line. The same thing happened with two other adults who had been pretending to be unacquainted. Finally, a third man excused himself from the line and admitted that he and his friends were also taking advantage of the single rider line but he’d rather not suffer the indignity of being found out and ejected.

Subscribe now

Obviously, none of this is a big deal. Despite what some on Bluesky might insist, I am not advocating that these people be drawn and quartered in the town square. But they activated a very particular pet peeve of mine, which is that even when rules seem small and inconsequential, breaking them for pure selfishness doesn’t only imply that the rule-breaker don’t care about the rules. It implies that they still want to enjoy a society where everyone else follows the rules, but they don’t, because they are special. And unlike fare evasion or shoplifting, these people cannot claim, even insincerely, that financial hardship or a rebellion against capitalism, AI, or Jeff Bezos was at the heart of their decision. They were at Disneyland!

I would argue, as I have before, that most people who evade fare or shoplift are also not doing it because they must steal to survive. Not to beat a dead stolen lemon, but when well-off writer Jia Tolentino notoriously joked about shoplifting a couple lemons from Whole Foods and people responded by confronting her outside her home, I thought that was a bit much. It was, after all, just lemons. But this behavior pissed people off (even if they went too far) precisely because Jia Tolentino (and other upper middle class people who steal for thrills, convenience, or for political statements) are not only stealing, but benefiting from a society where most people don’t steal. If literally every customer stole from Whole Foods instead of paying, there would simply be no Whole Foods, or the security would ramp up significantly to the point that shopping there would be very unpleasant (see: everything now locked up at CVS after people decided the rules didn’t apply to them). In that same interview, Hasan Piker defended shoplifting by pointing out that a certain amount of loss is baked into these businesses’ pricing model. That may be true, but it still assumes that only certain people will shoplifting. Why do you deserve to be in that subset but everyone else doesn’t?

The same is true, quite frankly, of Disney. Sure, things will not fall apart if only some people cut the lines. But why do you get to be one of those people?

Perhaps some rules are unnecessary and meant to be broken, but generally a good litmus test is: if everyone broke this rule, what would happen? Most of the time, you’ll find that if everyone broke a rule you’d like to break, the location where the rule-breaking took place would become completely unusable and descend into full CHAZ-tier anarchy. True, throwing a soda can on the ground should not earn you prison time, but if everyone littered all the time, the streets would be a disaster. Anyone who frequently litters has not just ignored a rule. They have decided that they are special and this rule doesn’t apply to them, but should still apply to everyone else (because surely, they don’t want to wade through two feet of empty hot Cheetos bags every day.)

The dog owner who proudly walks around town with an unleashed and aggressive dog is just taking a bet that other people will leash their own aggressive dogs, who might otherwise pose a danger to his. (And don’t get me started on the copious dog shit everywhere—I’m sure the people who allowed their dog to leave it are still very happy that other people are not smearing dog poop everywhere.) The person taking up two parking spots with her car has benefited from a parking space where everyone else only took up one. Sure, none of this should be jailable, but certainly we must do something. Genuinely, bring back this:

People who break these “minor” rules are essentially the same people who refused to do any work for their school projects, but still got to enjoy a good grade because the nerds stepped in and finished it for them. Most of society does not want bedlam; they will follow the rules even if other people don’t. But it doesn’t take many people to completely ruin an experience for the rule-followers.

I can’t help but notice that public spaces are made less convenient, less safe and less enjoyable because of selfish rule-breakers, or measures taken specifically to deter selfish rule-breakers. Thought you could enjoy the pretty fountain at the park? Well, you can’t, because someone threw garbage in the water and now it’s being drained for cleaning. Thought you could enjoy the donated plastic Barbie van at the park with your children? Well, you can’t, because someone lit it on fire and it melted onto the slide in spiky fragments, making the entire play structure unsafe until the city can come to fix it (yes, this actually happened near me a few years ago.) Oh, someone donated a little Fisher Price plastic food truck to the playground, so cute! Oh wait, a bunch of teenagers stomped on it overnight and now the park is littered in broken pieces of plastic. You thought you could enjoy a walk outside with your baby? Well, despite the “NO DOGS” sign, someone has shown up with his traumatized rescue pit bull who is “oh so friendly” and doesn’t need a leash.

It’s easy to call people like me crotchety Squidwards, but it doesn’t take that many people to devolve a society into a place where everything is filthy, unusable, unsafe or just unpleasant. Demonizing anyone (especially a woman) who stands up for these rules as a “Karen” has backfired, as now the Mrs. Crumplebottom elders of society who used to unofficially keep everyone in line by wagging their fingers at rule-breakers are too afraid to be recorded out of context. Assuming that anyone who breaks these rules is just poor has also backfired, since it’s abundantly clear that plenty of people break the rules for reasons that have nothing to do with financial hardship. The chess park is dead, the mural is vandalized, the playground is unusable, dog shit is all over the streets, adults are cutting children at Disneyland, but hey…at least the rule-breakers don’t have to be inconvenienced.

This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

You might also like…

item.title: Many Such Takes: Fart Corner, Men’s and Women’s Work, GTA 6, AOC, and More
item.description: The most unhinged discourse of the week, always free
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Many Such Takes, my twice-monthly roundup of Internet drama and discourse (mostly Twitter) and funny happenings online. If you enjoy a good guilty pleasure of unhinged discourse, this is for you. If it’s not your kind of thing, I implore you to check out my other recent articles, because while publishing 4-5 times a week, there’s always something for someone:

  • Internet culture: A Reddit Sub’s Ill-Fated Search for the Most Beautiful Vagina

  • Personal essay: How I told everyone in my elementary school that I was an alien in a human skin suit

  • Personal essay/culture: My own foray into looksmaxxing

  • Politics: The behaviors and tactics, not the positions, that defined Woke 1

  • Dating and relationships: The importance of looking like you have stuff going on and aren’t “the girl who dates on her birthday.”

  • Mental health: the one weird trick to fight OCD is to treat it like a demon

Consider becoming a free or paid subscriber for more!

Subscribe now

Fart Corner

This week, some local news from Georgia made quite a stink, so to speak: a teacher has a designated “fart corner” for students who need to pass gas, with the intention of normalizing this bodily function.

While she says the fart corner hasn’t resulted in any bullying or nonsense, apparently adults, myself included, cannot be so mature about it.

I have to admit, I have a hard time believing that kids aren’t making fun of each other for this. I used to be in a summer academic program, and this one girl farted loudly, and nobody knew who it was until she said, “Excuse me.” (It didn’t help that she had a lisp, pick a struggle.) Anyway, she never really lived it down, even though technically she was being polite. Everyone knows that when it comes to farting, you should just do it and then pretend it wasn’t you!

But while we’re spitballing here, I suggest we create a designated “nose picking station.”

GTA

In case you missed it, Grand Theft Auto 6 comes out November 19 and the trailer launched this week. The graphics are ultra-realistic and people are going nuts for it. But some people are taking the “nuts” part a bit too literally, claiming (or fantasizing) that we can have graphic sex in the game which somehow includes….fluids?

My honest reaction:

Others’ reactions:

No, no, let’s focus on the real problem here: the woman providing or extracting the fluids is merely a 6. Thwarted by the feminists oncemore!

Subscribe now

Men’s Work and Women’s Work

I didn’t post Many Such Takes last week on schedule because my entire TL was full of Lindsay Clancy discourse, and some things are just too horrible to be turned into a joke, but this week we finally got a reprieve because our top genderslop warriors turned to a new topic, courtesy (at least in part) of yours truly: the work that men and women do (or don’t do.)

It all started when I published the following article, which, TLDR, indicates that many women who choose to work full-time are doing it for the same reasons men are doing it (they like having money, and if they’re lucky, they also like their jobs even if they wouldn’t do it for free.)

I anticipated drama, but did not anticipate the particular type of drama that ensued. I thought that the men of Twitter might be offended by the idea that women had the same capacity for ambition as men, but in fact they went in the other direction and informed me that men (unlike women) hate their jobs, hate working, and would live in a dirty tent in the woods if anyone let them do it, but women are forcing them to go to the office. Eventually, this devolved to a bunch of guys insisting they’d rather be stay-at-home dads but men are forced to work and be miserable every minute of their lives, all so their wives can sit around at home presumably doing nothing.

That’s the thing about Twitter. Say what you will, but they will keep even the most seasoned, screen-addicted drama veteran a surprise!

Part of the drama was that some men seemed to be under the impression that all women are marketing executives, while all men are firefighters, resulting in the belief that of course women would enjoy their jobs more than men because women always have fun jobs with free matcha and men are always running into burning buildings.

Well, well, well, look whose article is relevant again

This culminated in…whatever this is:

Then, just as things were mercifully wrapping up, this quote from sociologist Susan Pickard dropped, “confirming” that there is simply no way for a woman to have kids and also be successful in her career. Oh no, NOT NOW SUSAN!

Now, while having lots of kids can be hard to swing with a career, many people of Twitter pointed out that actually, you can work and have kids, especially if your job doesn’t involve living on Mars for thirty years:

What a world, ! One can dream!

Subscribe now

Probiotic Pussy Eating

A viral funny tweet showed up on our TLs this week which spawned, say, not drama at all, just a lot of other tweets on the same topic. That topic: cunnilingus. See: above, GTA 6 fluids. It’s all connected!

Bryan Johnson, vampire billionaire who has meticulously measured his girlfriend’s “top 1% vagina” (in terms of healthy bacteria and pH of course) chimed in, because of course:

And now, a very novel take, that men who go down on women are actually just lacking in the necessary gut flora, with a side order of a racial pussy phrenology chart, which for all your sakes I will not include here. But more importantly, low bacterial diversity would, presumably, equal more odor! So much confidence for someone so misinformed on the vaginal microbiome!!

Also, at first I thought he was advocating for the consumption of vanilla-flavored vulva, but then I realized he meant “vanilla” now excludes oral sex?? (Well, on a woman, anyway.) Congrats everyone: you’re all kinky!

Anyway, I responded with my own Twitter troll post, in fact the last one I had ever posted—technically a friend’s, but I had sent him the text ahead of time and he posted as my proxy:

Ah, my Magnum Opus :*)

Subscribe now

Socially Gifted Autism

One piece of overlooked mini-drama this week: is it possible for an autistic person to have a form of autism that actually makes them extremely socially aware and gives them superhuman social cue detection abilities? Much to think about…

Quite a few commenters said they also had this “type” of autism, while other people threw out different, potentially overlapping diagnoses including but not limited to CPTSD, ADHD, anxiety, and OCD. Fuck it, why not ALL OF THE ABOVE?!

Or, perhaps, this is not actually a superhuman ability to detect social “queues” but rather, sensory overload:

The verdict from :

I chuckled at “my special interest is myself” because yo…that’s me as hell.

Hot Girls In Tech

Has anyone else noticed an abundance of people identifying as “Hot,” specifically in the San Francisco Bay Area?

I worked in the San Francisco tech scene for over a decade, and an abundance of Hot Girls was absolutely not my experience, at least not when it came to actual tech employees. Nobody would have dared call themselves a “hot girl in tech” because to do so would have A.) invited people to inform them that they weren’t as hot as they thought and B.) subjected them to general ridicule. We had female founders, who perhaps emphasized the fact that they were women (being a girlboss wasn’t always a bad thing, you know) and we certainly had women in tech who were incidentally hot, but Hot Girls In Tech was not a thing.

The other day, tech founder Georgia Witchel penned an essay on Twitter about a sudden rise in viral “hot girls in tech” posts, where a woman will post something about her arrival to the tech scene but the post will be more about her own hotness than anything she’s actually doing in tech:

She was not, however, condemning these women, instead pointing out that they were engaging in a form of influencing/marketing and should be left alone to do their thing.

Then, another female founder, Claire Vo, stepped in to let everyone know that actually, it’s really hard to be so beautiful while also being so smart, and to salute the “sisterhood of hot tech girls:”

People seemed particularly focused on this section of her long-form tweet, where she felt unwelcome in a computer science classroom in part because she was the only woman, but also because everyone else was so fugly:

While some people agreed with her that women are underestimated in tech when they are conventionally attractive, reactions were mixed:

Aaaand I see we’ve now reached the “look how young everyone thinks I am” one-upping part of the discourse. Right on schedule!

This guy took a stab at his own male copypasta version of the tweet, paragraph by paragraph, noting that as a “gigachad” in tech, nobody but him cared about optimal bone structure and he felt locked out of a room that might have well said “no hot guys alllowed, manlets only.”

Subscribe now

AOC

Now, after all that genderslop and slop (misc: other), I almost forgot to cover anything political. But don’t worry, because I somehow have a political story that is still genderslop.

Earlier this month, AOC posted a video of administering injections for egg freezing, warning viewers (ie: people on the Internet) not to “be weird.” Good luck with that one!

But many denizens of Twitter were more confused about why she would freeze eggs when she’s been in a relationship for over a decade—and engaged to the guy for more than four years.

As it turns out, they broke up before the egg freezing. With AOC now single and entertaining a 2028 presidential run, she’s put herself in possibly the most confusing and psychosexual place on Twitter.

I actually do not mind or judge AOC’s egg-freezing journey videos, in part because I underwent a similar process when my husband and I did IVF, and I posted about it a lot. When you’re undergoing any kind of fertility treatment, you can really feel like you’re the only one in the world doing it, and seeing other people in your boat can make you feel better! That said, I did wonder if these videos would be a net negative for her odds at a 2028 primary win, especially since many people on Twitter were saying things like this:

Yeah, to be honest, this person is not screaming “Democratic Primary Voter.”

In fact, according to Polymarket, AOC is now the most favored candidate for the 2028 Democratic Primary:

Was it the egg freezing? The breakup? Denouncing “Woke 1?” The potential of a mass wave of horny primary voters? Or maybe just that…a lot of people like her and always have? Given that JD Vance is the clear favorite for the Republican nomination, I’m not sure we’re ready for the most terminally online general election ever. Well, I’m ready. Maybe Many Such Takes will have to become weekly again.

This segment part of a data partnership with Polymarket.

Funny Tweets/Other Happenings

Right wing Twitter discovered the concept of “the linear passage of 25 years:”

Musical satirist Kyle Gordon has finally parodied the music of my youth, but unfortunately the song is just way too catchy:

Someone is trying to rain (quite literally) on Dr. Smells’ parade:

And, whatever this is:

item.title: Hipsters Dominated an Era By Being Easy Targets
item.description: Being the only niche subculture at which you could “punch up” helped hipsters define the culture of a decade.
item.content:encoded:
The Weird Al of our generation, Kyle Gordon, is out with another musical “parody” that is somehow too good to be truly satirical. “I’m A Whore” perfectly encapsulates the type of music that I listened to in the early 2010s while serving “Jell-O shots” which was actually a Tupperware of lime Jell-O made with tequila, petrified with a couple of loose strings of cilantro. “I’m A Whore” is so nostalgic for me that I’ve been listening to it constantly and trying my best not to sing “getting fucked in a rusty dumpster” at the UPS store. And when Kyle Gordon first tweeted a preview of his song, he titled it with none other than a single year: 2010.

The viral nature of this, frankly, major banger, has brought up 2010s nostalgia once again. Technically, “I’m a Whore” is more indie sleaze than hipster, but the two were definitely connected (and some would say, more of a square-rectangle situation than two unique subcultures.) And while plenty of things were big in the early 2010s—business casual clubwear, birds on everything, iridescent backpacks at Coachella, God help me, the hipsters are still the emblem that I find the most evocative of this time in history, specifically the late 2000s to mid 2010s. Nothing screams 2010 more than an arrogant guy with a handlebar mustache and pastel suspenders, bringing a rotary phone on the subway so everyone can see how ironic he is.

So how did one small subculture—a subculture, in fact, who prided themselves on being ironic and hard for the masses to understand—become the dominant cultural force of a decade? I’ll tell you: by being really easy to mock, and being privileged enough, per 2010s standards, that nobody felt bad about mocking them.

Subscribe now

I have a great deal of experience with hipsters, given that I have spent time in New York City and San Francisco, between the years 2005 and 2016. This is basically like saying you lived in Uzbekistan in the early 1200s and were at least somewhat acquainted with Genghis Khan’s army. As a result, I know what made hipsters such an interesting subculture that everyone sought to write about them and parody them, from Kyle Gordon to Portlandia to the viral 2009 Tumblr LATFH (Look At This Fucking Hipster) which was later turned into a book. The easiest way to get a laugh, circa 2010, was to make a joke about hipsters. They were the perfect punch line—ridiculous, goofy, visually identifiable, and most importantly, not terribly downtrodden, so nobody felt that bad for making fun of them. In fact, they probably thought they were better than you.

Hipsters were counter-cultural, but in a way that didn’t apply to the punks and Goths of yore. Hipsters weren’t rebelling against the mainstream—they were simply too good for it. To be a hipster was to be above it all, to use a fax machine ironically, to do everything with a hint of derision and “you wouldn’t get it.” Hipsters were into music you have never heard of, not because the music was weird and edgy but because you weren’t cultured enough to get the reference. Hipsters wore clothes you might have found odd, not because they wanted to shock you but because they were plugged into a world you could never dream of understanding. And to make fun of hipsters was to “punch up,” because arrogance was part of their whole deal. Suddenly, a new extremely ripe genre for parody fell into the laps of every comedian, satirist and blogger.

Importantly, hipsters never publicly identified as such. To identify as a hipster, or even admit knowledge of hipsters, was to eject yourself from the in-group. A Goth kid might have worn a flame-embellished T-shirt that literally spelled out the word “Goth,” (ie: me in seventh grade) but a hipster would never dream of wearing a quirky cardigan that spelled out “Hipster.” The first rule of hipsterdom was that you had to deny being one. Obviously, this changed over time—but in the 2000s, the “hipster who insists they aren’t a hipster” was a common meme. It was even mentioned in the 2013 movie, This is the End, where Jay Baruchel’s hipster-adjacent character denies being a hipster, while his friends quiz him on all the mainstream things on which he looks down. It was also parodied on The Onion.

In college, I had a brief encounter with a flock of hipsters which has stuck with me for almost twenty years. During freshman orientation week in 2007, I made the mistake of getting extremely drunk at a party. A few hipsters—including their leader, a guy in an ironic ascot and tweed blazer who went by the pseudonym “Hymen Cavendish”—took notice of me and absconded with me to their dorm, along with an equally confused freshman boy in a popped collar polo shirt named Dave.

Dave and I had landed in the den of the hipsters: a place so exclusive and so shrouded in mystery that it felt almost dreamlike, a place to which surely, countless other freshmen who wrote bad poetry had been denied access. But we were not only there. We were taken by force. We were the hipsters’ concubines. As we sat there on the dumpy second-hand velvet couch, staring at Hymen Cavendish and his band of merry thieves smoking cigarettes, we couldn’t help but wonder what they wanted with us. Was the latest hipster trend a fedora fashioned from freshman skin?

I have limited recollection of that night, but I remember that Dave and I were brought in as a form of entertainment for the hipsters, who treated us the way Russian royalty in the 1700s might have treated a dancing bear. We may have literally been asked to dance at one point. We were also asked all sorts of questions, and they laughed at our answers, even if they weren’t funny. I realized I was probably being used for some kind of joke, the way a bunch of drunk adults might ask a toddler, “What’s the worst word you know?” but Dave and I were too drunk and out-of-the-loop to understand. We continued to accept the free drinks they continually shoved in our faces.

The hipsters let us sleep over on their couches, and the next morning at around 7 AM, they roused us, dressed us in insanely preppy clothing which they had lying around, took us outside and snapped a bunch of photos of us near the trees meant to satirize the humorless, irony-free, painfully preppy school magazine. At the end of the ordeal, I recall feeling used and weird, but not fully understanding why. Nobody had touched me or said anything hurtful, but for a full twelve hours I was made painfully aware of how little I was in on the joke. This was an overdose of the hipster experience. Most people just got a vague sense that hipsters looked down on them, sans kidnapping.

These same hipsters published a daily school pamphlet meant to be satirical (with Hymen Cavendish as editor in chief) but their jokes were always so esoteric and weird that the student body didn’t understand them and repeatedly groaned that it was pretentious. One day, the daily pamphlet was literally just a photocopied image of Jafar from Aladdin. When people failed to get the joke, the hipsters pretended to have abandoned the publication and handed it over to student government. Then, they proceeded to write terribly corny “normal” content for several weeks while pretending to be the staff of the school magazine, only to reveal that only idiots would have enjoyed the fake normal-person pamphlet.

I have to admit, they were cooking with that one.

But you can see why people made fun of them, if only because “they made fun of us first” seemed like a good enough reason. But that wasn’t the only reason that hipsters became an easy target. The start of Woke 1 (see: early to mid 2010s) meant that the list of acceptable mockery targets in comedy and parody was dwindling, in some ways for the better. And this shift happened pretty quickly—I Now Pronounce You Chuck and Larry came out in 2007, and the movie followed two straight men pretending to be gay-married for life insurance purposes, complete with Rob Schneider portraying an egregiously racist caricature of an Asian person. Just a few short years later, it would be unfathomable for such a movie to be green lit. By the 2010s, aware that casual racism, homophobia, sexism and perhaps not even fatphobia were going to fly as much, mainstream comedy writers, satirists and comedians realized hipsters were a much safer and funnier punching bag with mass appeal.

Hipsters were typically white, upper middle class, and straight—literally the only fully acceptable target during Woke 1. In fact, when I typed “hipster” into the search bar for Substack royalty-free images, almost every image was of a thin white man. Suddenly, every comedy writer who wanted to mock people but didn’t want to say anything bigoted had an easy way out. And to make matters even easier, hipsters never admitted to being hipsters, so even they could not get offended, at least not publicly. Not that anyone was particularly worried about offending white men in the 2010s, but these jokes also weren’t offensive to white men in general, because most white men weren’t hipsters. In fact, many of the biggest lampooners of hipsters were upper middle class white men themselves.

The End of Austin, an Austin-based independent news site and blog, noted in 2016:

We hate hipsters don’t we? It’s probably their detached air of superiority that irks us most, but in reality, we hate it all.

They also acknowledged that social justice issues that were popular to discuss in the early 2010s contributed to the mockery of hipsters. Not only were hipsters privileged and therefore fair game, but they were supposedly actively harming others:

The liberal-arts-grad social justice bloggers began their anti-hipster campaigns. Hipsters became targets of sweeping erudite critiques. Hipsters were suddenly sexist, racist, privileged purveyors of cultural appropriation. They caused East Side gentrification. They perpetuated rape culture. They scandalously fooled the world into buying fake bean-to-bar chocolate.

This was a fair characterization of the 2010s social justice oriented hipster hate wave. The pre-polycule-scandal Lindy West penned a famous essay about “hipster racism” asserting that hipsters were ironically being racist as a way to be racist for real. In it, she used the example of Zooey Deschanel ironically using the hashtag #thuglife about herself on Twitter, among others. This was also the accusation leveraged against the hipster DJ who hosted Kill Whitey parties, which he said were intended to ironically make fun of white people, but others felt these events were a way to ironically make fun of Black people making fun of white people. In Vice, Noel Ransome said that he hated hipster racists more than “hicks” who shout racial slurs. Lena Dunham also caught accusations of hipster racism in 2017, the only evidence being that she was reportedly friends with a girl in college who said a racial slur “ironically.” Academic Robin James asserted that the very concept of something being hip was racist: “Discourses of taste and hipness produce individual bodies as white, and maintain Whiteness as a socio-political norm.”

Hipster racism was a real thing, and some hipsters absolutely were “ironically racist.” But this reputation eventually meant that all hipsters were fair game for the accusation (and associated mockery) under the guise of social justice.

But the hipster, even as our cultural punchline, eventually started to go mainstream in metropolitan areas. In a way, going mainstream was the worst possible thing to happen to a hipster, far more upsetting than being mocked on Portlandia. Is a hipster still a hipster if he is the dominant cultural force and not something niche and ironic?

This was when “hipster” stopped meaning “weird theatrical guy in a retro costume who wants everyone to call him Hymen” and started meaning “upper middle class tech worker who likes artisanal cocktails.” A bit niche, but far more accessible, and predictably visible from the street as every “bacon-cupcake food truck” drove by the offices of some doomed startup called Vooka or Blamify or something else stupid. Part of this transition was simply that hipsters were getting older. And no matter how ironic and weird you are at twenty, the curse of the unc comes for us all. Even Hymen Cavendish.

Hipsters probably had to tone down some of the weirdness and quirky behavior to survive as adults, especially adults with normal jobs. Perhaps some people still found them pretentious as they slapped mint leaves to release the essence as part of their painfully expensive mason jar Moscow mule recipe. But “you probably never heard of it” eventually transitioned into “I made it myself,” which is a lot less abrasive. Thus, people who previously either didn’t like, didn’t understand, or didn’t know any hipsters were able to engage with this new sanitized “hipster culture.” And who didn’t want to eat homemade stone-ground mustard? Even if someone was a bit pretentious about it, wasn’t it nice for them to take pleasure in making things?

By the mid to late 2010s, the “hipster” had gone beyond normalcy and into painfully-uncool-mainstream territory, which was antithetical to the ethos of the hipster. It was no longer about being obscure and niche, or about knowing things nobody else knew. If anything, hipsters retreated from the pretentious and rapidly barreled toward corny, if not totally cheugy. It’s striking that mainstream bands like fun, Mumford & Sons, and their corny “stomp clap hey” music became synonymous with hipsters—Hymen Cavendish would never.

The hipster aesthetic going mainstream in the 2010s meant that the original hipsters—the ones who reveled in being into stuff nobody else was into—had to abandon their schtick. They either became mainstream “hipsters” themselves as they matured (thereby no longer really being hipsters) or they had to start doing something else to continue being sufficiently countercultural. I tried to look up Hymen Cavendish to see what he’s up to now, but I realized I actually don’t know his real name.

In 2009, the hipster was the obnoxious-as-shit guy in your literature class, but by 2017, he was your friendly neighborhood barista, your coworker, the bagel guy who made the bagels with the homemade kimchi aioli. How can you make fun of these wholesome pillars of the community?

Now in the 2020s, things like craft breweries, home canning, modern farmhouse decor, food trucks, beards and tattoos are, if anything, painfully normal. Not even urban, not even mainstream-cool. They are the trademark of a city block that’s been “gentrified.” They are the Austin Instagram momfluencer’s favorite things. They are, dare I say, apparently the worst thing in the world: millennial. The male hipster aesthetic of suspenders, beards and undercuts is so conventional that it no longer gives off Portland, it gives off tweets that say, “A truly based patriarch doesn’t let his wife wear shoes” from a man with Christian/husband/father in his bio. What was once meant to look ironically old-fashioned has come full circle and now is more of an aesthetic you’d see among Christian polygamy influencers.

But young, cool, “you’ve never heard of it” people still exist. Perhaps the young people hoping to revive indie sleaze (or parody it) are this generation’s hipsters. But I think the hipster era was a unique cultural moment in that hipsters rose to popularity during a time when the Internet enabled the exchange of trends and music (but was still not so diffuse as it is today) so that all the pretentious kids could more or less settle on the same schtick. But I think as long as cities and young people exist, there will be a certain cohort of obnoxious young people who think anything normal is stupid, and anything weird is cool, and if you can’t tell the difference, skill issue, as they say. (No need to remind me that they no longer say this.)

But for whatever reason, these young people are not so central to our zeitgeist. Maybe they’re being ironic but nobody knows about it. (If a hipster makes a reference nobody gets, but nobody is even there to hear it, is he really a hipster at all?) People make fun of Gen Z, but not for being hipsters—just for not leaving their houses and being afraid of making phone calls. Even then, the jokes have nothing on the hipster jokes. Nobody is making a coffee table book of Gen Z shut-ins. If hipsters exist today, nobody seems aware of their existence, at least not as a cohesive cultural emblem, because they just aren’t as fun to mock.
